quote: This connects two prior BERIL findings: the `amr_fitness_cost` project showed mechanism predicts conservation (metal 44% accessory vs efflux 13% core), and we now show this conservation pattern is driven by ecology — efflux genes are core because they serve host-associated organisms constitutively, while metal resistance is accessory because it varies with environmental metal exposure.
heading: Different niches select for different resistance strategies

text: The report states that AMR accumulation varies within bacterial species depending on where strains are found.

quote: The 14% of families with significant within-family effects are the most convincing evidence, but most families don't span enough environments to test.
heading: Limitations

text: NCBI overrepresentation of clinical isolates and undersampling of soil and aquatic species partly confound the finding that clinical species carry more AMR, because clinical species are sequenced in part because they have AMR.
quote: Clinical isolates are massively overrepresented in NCBI. The "clinical species carry more AMR" finding partly reflects that clinical species are the ones that get sequenced because they have AMR. Soil and aquatic species are undersampled.
heading: Limitations

text: Majority-vote species environment classification collapses within-species variation and can label species containing environmental strains as clinical; sensitivity analysis at 60-90% thresholds mitigates this limitation.
quote: The majority-vote species-level classification collapses within-species variation. A species classified as "clinical" may include environmental strains. The sensitivity analysis at 60-90% thresholds mitigates this.
heading: Limitations

text: AMRFinderPlus focuses on known resistance genes and may underestimate novel resistance in environmental bacteria, biasing the report toward more AMR in clinical species with well-characterized resistance genes.
quote: AMRFinderPlus focuses on known resistance genes, potentially underestimating novel resistance in environmental bacteria. This would bias our results toward finding more AMR in clinical species (where resistance genes are well-characterized).
heading: Limitations

text: The 95% prevalence threshold for core AMR depends on species genome count, and small genome counts make many species' core/accessory labels imprecise.
quote: The 95% prevalence threshold for "core" depends on species genome count. Many species have few genomes, making core/accessory labels imprecise.
heading: Limitations

text: The report observes correlation rather than causation between environment and AMR, with antibiotic exposure and virulence-resistance co-selection offered as alternative causal explanations.
quote: We observe correlation between environment and AMR, not causation. Clinical species may carry more AMR because they are clinical (antibiotic exposure), or they may be clinical because they carry more AMR (virulence-resistance co-selection).
heading: Limitations

text: Although all tests are highly significant (p ~ 0), environment effects on AMR composition are modest (η² = 0.02–0.13), explaining 2-13% of variance, while phylogeny likely explains much more.
quote: While all tests are highly significant (p ~ 0), the effect sizes are modest (η² = 0.02–0.13). Environment explains 2-13% of variance in AMR composition — phylogeny likely explains much more.
heading: Limitations

text: The report excluded 18.7% of AMR clusters (15,550) lacking mechanism classification from H3 mechanism fractions, potentially biasing results if their environment distribution is non-random.
quote: 18.7% of AMR clusters (15,550) could not be classified to a mechanism. These are excluded from H3 mechanism fractions, potentially biasing the analysis if unclassified genes are non-randomly distributed across environments.
heading: Limitations
